title: Mini-runbook: GPU pod pressure surge (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, pragmatic runbook for incidents that look like: sudden GPU pod pressure (OOMs, long queue times, token surge causing kv-cache thrash) on a subset of serving nodes. Focus is on triage, short-term mitigation, safe node replacement (hardware or VM reprovision), and controlled capacity additions with model warmup to avoid repeated thrash.

Status: draft. This is intentionally conversational — notes-to-self, commands, and open questions included. Use and iterate.

1) Quick triage (first 10 minutes)
- Slack: @oncall-pager -> announce "GPU pod pressure, high queueing on model X, investigating". Ping infra-runbooks channel and svc-owner (product-hosted-api).
- Dashboard check (Console -> Per-route latency + tokens): identify affected model(s), zones, and node labels.
- Prometheus quick queries:
  - 95p_latency = histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(redwood_request_duration_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le, route, model))
  - gpu_util = avg(node_gpu_utilization{cluster="prod"}) by (node)  // look for >95% sustained
  - pod_restarts = increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[15m])
  - kv_cache_hit = rate(redwood_kv_cache_hit_total[1m]) / rate(redwood_kv_cache_request_total[1m])
- Determine if a single node or many nodes are affected. If only a single node shows high GPU util + OOMs, treat as node-level; otherwise, consider workload-wide surge or autoscaler misconfig.

2) Immediate mitigation (stop bleeding)
- If model-level throttling is available: enable temporary rate limit on the offending route(s) (Console -> route throttles). Aim to reduce ingress by ~30–50% to let queues drain.
- If ingress throttling not possible: use traffic routing policy to shift a small percentage of traffic to fallback model variant (lower-memory/quantized) or to another region. Can use canary routing: set 10–20% fallback, increase if necessary.
- If one node is overloaded: cordon + drain with low-impact flags. Commands (kubectl):
  - kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector=status.phase=Running -n redwood | grep <node-name>
  - kubectl cordon <node-name>
  - kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m
  Note: prefer graceful drain with shorter grace period during pressure to speed up eviction, but preserve critical in-flight KV cache if possible.
- Watch autoscaler: if cluster-autoscaler is enabled, temporarily set max as appropriate or pause scale-to-zero jobs to avoid thrash during replacement.

3) Safe-replace (hardware swap or reprovision)
- If node diagnosed as GPU-hardware degraded (NVML errors, ECC errors): schedule replacement. For on-prem, follow hardware acceptance checklist; for cloud, reprovision instance with the same GPU SKU.
- Pre-replacement checklist:
  - Confirm node is drained and unschedulable.
  - Verify no long-running model snapshots pinned to that node (check redwood_kv_cache_owner label). If some cache owners exist, coordinate with model-serving to persist or accept cache loss.
  - Snapshot node diagnostics: dmesg, nvidia-smi -q, system logs (store in /tmp/incident-logs/<node>-<ts>.tgz) and upload to RED-7891.
- Replacement steps (cloud VM):
  1. Terminate old instance after drain completes.
  2. Launch new instance with identical kernel and GPU drivers (use golden image).
  3. Run smoke: nvidia-smi, run gpu-bench-single.sh (5m), run health-checks (redwood-infra/acceptance).
  4. Label node with version and acceptance: kubectl label node <node> redwood/acceptance=2025-11-07
  5. Uncordon node when smoke looks good: kubectl uncordon <node>
  6. Observe scheduling gradually (do not uncordon more than 1 node per zone in parallel).
- Replacement steps (physical GPU swap):
  1. Coordinate with datacenter ops and schedule a maintenance window if not emergent.
  2. Quiesce traffic: enable route throttles and drain node first.
  3. Power down node per hardware SOP, swap GPU, reseat connectors, check firmware.
  4. Power on, run GPU acceptance tests (nvml check + model smoke).
  5. Reintroduce to cluster as above.

4) Capacity add + warmup (to avoid immediate thrash)
- When adding capacity (hot-add or scale-up), avoid letting the autoscaler immediately flood new nodes with cold model workloads. New nodes need kernel selection + kv-cache warmup. Suggested sequence:
  1. Add nodes with taints: kubectl taint nodes <new-node> redwood/warmup=true:NoSchedule
  2. Start a small set of warmed-up pods on each new node using a job that preloads models and runs a set of canonical prompts (we call this the warmup harness). Use lower concurrency.
  3. Validate model kernel selection logs (redwood_runtime_kernel) and that quantization path is selected correctly.
  4. Remove warmup taint and gradually increase traffic allocation (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% over 30–60 minutes), monitoring latency and kv cache hit.
- Warmup harness notes: run 100–300 short requests across top-5 prompt shapes seen in the incident window; record kv_cache_hit and initial token latency. If cache hit < 0.2 after warmup, extend warmup run.

5) Post-incident review (PIR / mini postmortem)
- Collect: graphs, node diagnostics tarball, kube events, route configs, autoscaler logs. Attach to RED-7891.
- Short PIR template (for the incident doc):
  - Summary of impact (routes, p95 latency, duration).
  - Timeline of actions (timestamps, person).
  - Root cause hypothesis (hardware vs load pattern vs software bug).
  - Short-term mitigations applied and their effectiveness.
  - Long-term actions (owner + due date).
  - Communication notes (customer impact, CS handoff).
- Typical long-term actions from GPU pod pressure incidents:
  - Improve warmup harness coverage for top models (owner: eng-serving-runtime).
  - Add route-level auto-throttle thresholds and automated fallback routing (owner: product-hosted-api).
  - Enhance node health export to include NVLML ECC counters to detect pre-failure (owner: infra).

6) Common troubleshooting commands & hints
- Check GPU errors: ssh node && sudo journalctl -u nvidia-persistenced -n 200
- NVML errors: sudo /usr/bin/nvidia-smi -q | egrep "(ECC|Xid|Error)" -A2
- Check pods stuck Terminating: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces | grep Terminating
- Force delete only if safe: kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=0 --force (avoid if pod holds stateful cache)
- Look for oom_kill: sudo dmesg | grep -i oom
- Check unexpected kernel selection fallback: kubectl logs <pod> -c runner | grep "fallback-kernel"

7) Communication checklist
- Internal: update incident channel with short updates every 15 minutes during mitigation.
- Customer-facing: coordinate with CS if p99 latency breaches SLA for >30m. Prepare templated messaging with impact + ETA.
- Postmortem publish: 48–72 hours after incident, with owners and implementation plan for followups.

8) Open questions / TODOs (record for next revision)
- Should we automate warmup taint + harness when cluster-autoscaler adds nodes? (Pros: prevents immediate thrash; Cons: slower scale-up)
- Can we persist/restore kv-cache across node reprovisions for hot models? (complex, but huge win for latency)
- Add a tiny sidecar that reports NVML ECC counters into node exporter (owner: observability).
- Playbook automation: wrap safe-replace steps into a runbook script to reduce time-to-unblock for oncall.

Notes to oncall: this doc is intentionally compact; use the full infra playbooks for hardware replacement if present. If anything is unclear, call Marcus or Priya first — they own the warmup harness and acceptance tests.

Revision history:
- 2025-11-07: initial draft (Aisha)
- 2025-12-02: added warmup harness guidance and acceptance smoke steps (Marcus)
